subtopic: Representation and Graph of a Function
stem: Using the graph of \(y = g(x)\) given below, find \(g(-4)\) and \(g(3)\). (In the figure each grid square is 2 units along both axes. The curve rises from the lower left through the marked points \((-6,\,-4)\) and \((-4,\,0)\) to a local maximum at the marked point \((-1,\,4)\), then falls to a local minimum near \(x = 3\), and rises again, crossing the X-axis near \(x = 9\).)
solution:
[Textbook error, answer-affecting: the printed solution states "From graph when \(x = 3\), \(y = -5\) so \(g(3) = -5\)", but that disagrees with the book's OWN figure. On Fig. 6.14 the curve's minimum marker sits at the same height on the page as the labelled point \((-6, -4)\) — two points at the same height have the same \(y\)-value — so the minimum is at \(y \approx -4\), and \(g(3) \approx -4\), a full unit above the printed value. The companion reading \(g(-4) = 0\) is confirmed correct by the figure.]

From graph when \(x = -4\), \(y = 0\)
so \(g(-4) = 0\)
From graph when \(x = 3\), \(y = -5\) so \(g(3) = -5\)
diagramNote: Fig. 6.14 (printed p.109, bottom of the left column) — the graph of \(y = g(x)\) on a square grid whose every square is 2 units on both axes. Marked points: \((-6,-4)\), \((-4,0)\), \((-1,4)\) (labelled), plus three unlabelled markers at the local minimum, on the rising right branch, and at the right-hand X-axis crossing. Load-bearing: \(g(3)\) cannot be obtained without the figure.
_note: BOOK DEFECT CANDIDATE — printed solution disagrees with the book's own figure. The solution states 'From graph when x = 3, y = -5 so g(3) = -5'. Fig. 6.14 was pixel-measured against its own grid: the gridlines are uniform at 44.5 px and the origin is exact, and calibrating on all three LABELLED points gives 1 square = 2 units on both axes with each labelled point accurate to within 0.15 units — measured (-6.00, -3.88), (-4.06, -0.02), (-1.10, 4.14). At that accuracy the plotted curve at x = 3 reads y = -4.2, and the unlabelled marker at the local minimum reads (3.28, -4.38), whose nearest lattice point is (3, -4), NOT (3, -5). So -5 is not readable off the printed grid; the discrepancy (0.6-0.8 units) is 4-5x the figure's own drafting error. Transcribed exactly as printed per the brief; flagged for the answer-key cross-check pass to adjudicate whether the printed -5 or the drawn figure is wrong. Also note the stem+figure sit at the BOTTOM of the left column while this Solution sits at the TOP of the right column (column-wise straddle).
The book prints the sub-heading 'Function Solution:' immediately before this example. Factorisation and both roots independently re-derived and correct.

subtopic: Representation and Graph of a Function
stem: From the graph below find \(x\) for which \(f(x) = 4\). (Fig. 6.15 shows \(y = f(x)\), an upward-opening parabola whose vertex touches the X-axis at \((1,\,0)\), drawn on a unit grid with the X-axis marked from \(-2\) to \(5\) and the Y-axis marked \(1\) to \(5\), together with the horizontal line \(y = 4\).)
solution:
To solve \(f(x) = 4\) i.e. \(y = 4\)
Find the values of \(x\) where graph intersects line \(y = 4\).
Therefore, \(x = -1\) and \(x = 3\).
diagramNote: Fig. 6.15 (printed p.109, right column) — \(y = f(x)\), an upward parabola with vertex at \((1,0)\) on the X-axis, with the horizontal line \(y = 4\) drawn across it. Fig. 6.16 (same page, lower right) is the solution figure: the same graph redrawn, with the two intersections of the curve and \(y = 4\) to be read off. Either figure alone answers the question.
_note: STRADDLES THE PAGE BOUNDARY. The stem, Fig. 6.15, the 'Solution :' opening and Fig. 6.16 are all on p-03 (printed p.109); the concluding line 'Therefore, x = -1 and x = 3.' is the FIRST line of the left column of p-04 (printed p.110), above the 'Function from equation:' heading. Both halves are transcribed here. Figure verified by inspection: the vertex sits exactly on the X-axis at x = 1 and the curve meets y = 4 at the gridlines x = -1 and x = 3, consistent with f(x) = (x-1)^2, so the printed answer is correct.

subtopic: Representation and Graph of a Function
solution:
Given equation is \(4x + 7y = 1\)
From the given equation
\(7y = 1 - 4x\)
\(y = \frac{1 - 4x}{7}\) = function of \(x\)
So \(y = f(x) = \frac{1 - 4x}{7}\)
_note: The book labels this example 'Ex. 5) (Activity)' under the heading 'Function from equation:'. Its printed solution is a fill-in-the-blank scaffold — in part (i) three empty boxes, printed as '7y = [ ]', 'y = [ ] = function of x' and 'So y = f(x) = [ ]'. The result is fully determinate, so per the shipped Class-11/Class-12 precedent for numbered Activity examples the blanks are COMPLETED here: 1 - 4x, (1-4x)/7 and (1-4x)/7 respectively are DERIVED, not printed in the book.

subtopic: Representation and Graph of a Function
solution:
Given equation is \(4x + 7y = 1\)
From the given equation
\(4x = 1 - 7y\)
\(x = \frac{1 - 7y}{4}\) = function of \(y\)
So \(x = g(y) = \frac{1 - 7y}{4}\)
_note: Part (ii) of the same 'Ex. 5) (Activity)'. Its printed solution likewise carries three empty boxes: '4x = [ ]', 'x = [ ] = function of y' and 'So x = g(y) = [ ]'. Completed here: 1 - 7y, (1-7y)/4 and (1-7y)/4 are DERIVED, not printed in the book.
